newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends softer in US on trade fears, EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends softer in US on trade fears, EMU pact.

text.p: *Dollar ends lower vs yen, mark in quiet trade.
*Dlr/mark hurt after selling on news of EU stability pact
deal, dealers booked profits from Friday's dollar rally.
*Yen jumpy pre-G7 summit, with Japan, US trade data Tue-Thur.
*Rubin says world wants more open Japanese markets, financial liberalization. Traders see nothing new in remark, dollar unfazed.

Dollar/yen ended lower in quiet trade after fears of Japanese trade surpluses took hold, while a deal struck by European leaders to stabilize budgets after monetary union left dollar/mark limp, dealers said.

Against the yen, the dollar continued overnight losses, ending at its session low as the market prepared for swelling Japanese trade deficits to be a hot topic when leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations meet in Denver for a three-day summit on Friday.
Import/Export data from both Japan and the United States will be released before the gathering.

"The summit is this weekend, hence dollar/yen will probably be more of a focus of trading this week, now that the stability pact is out," said Stephen Flanagan, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Credit Agricole Indosuez.
The dollar ended at 113.24/29 yen, down from 113.66/71 at the open and 114.80/90 at Friday's close. Dollar/mark was at 1.7305/15,off a touch from its 1.7310/20 U.S. open.
Figures out Tuesday are expected to show Japan's trade surplus grew in May, while April U.S. data out Thursday are forecast to reveal the opposite -- a wider deficit.
"We continue to view dollar/yen as a politically-charged currency again. Any increase in the surplus should bring in selling pressure on dollar/yen," Flanagan said.
But the markets showed little reaction to remarks by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who said on Monday the world wants Japan to open markets more and push financial liberalization.

The dollar's four-day rally against the German currency last week ended when profit-taking set in after EU finance ministers reached a compromise deal Monday on limiting budget deficits after the launch of Europe's single currency.
Dollar/mark was also hurt, touching a U.S. low of 1.7280, and dollar/yen was buoyed by a brief bout of mark/yen buying.
The budget agreement incorporated French demands for a resolution on employment and growth.

Last week, anticipation of an accord bolstered confidence that monetary union would go forward as scheduled in 1999, helping the dollar by raising the odds the mark would lose its dominant role in Europe to a weaker currency, the euro.
France and Germany were sharply divided over the issue after France's new left-wing government balked at signing the pact, negotiated late last year.

"The stability pact was signed with very little impact in European trading markets. (It was) pretty much as expected, an addendum with jobs was attached to it," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.
Elsewhere, the dollar inched up to 1.4420/30 Swiss from 1.4415/25 and rose to Canadian $1.3864/69 from C$1.3780/85.
The pound also firmed to $1.6368/78, from $1.6360/70.
The Australian dollar fell to $0.7484/89 from $0.7513/18.
((--Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
